name: New Orleans
title: Holidays in New Orleans
intro: Jazz on every corner, a paddle steamer on the Mississippi and beignets for breakfast. Here's what New Orleans is like with the family and when to go.
facts_note: Check entry rules on GOV.UK before you book.
when_to_go: March, April, October and November are warm and dry, with lots of festivals. Mardi Gras in February or March is spectacular, with family-friendly parades away from the French Quarter. Summer is hot and sticky, and hurricane season peaks from August to October.

things.name: French Quarter
things.blurb: Street musicians, balconies and Jackson Square by day. Bourbon Street isn't for children at night.

things.name: Café du Monde
things.blurb: Hot beignets covered in icing sugar, open almost round the clock.

things.name: Steamboat Natchez
things.blurb: A paddle steamer cruise on the Mississippi with live jazz.

things.name: Swamp tour
things.blurb: A boat through the bayou to spot alligators.

things.name: Audubon Zoo
things.blurb: Rare white alligators and a Louisiana swamp area.

things.name: City Park
things.blurb: Old oak trees, Storyland playground and a vintage carousel.

faqs.question: Is New Orleans good for a family holiday?
faqs.answer: Yes, for families who love music and food. Daytime is very family-friendly, while some areas get rowdy late at night.

faqs.question: How many nights do you need?
faqs.answer: Four or five nights, or combine it with Nashville or Memphis on a music road trip.

faqs.question: Do UK families need a visa?
faqs.answer: Most British passport holders, children included, apply for an ESTA online before they fly rather than a visa. Check GOV.UK for the current rules.

faqs.question: Is Mardi Gras OK for children?
faqs.answer: Yes, on the parade routes uptown along St. Charles Avenue, where families bring ladders and catch beads. Avoid the French Quarter at night.
